draft.change: Add the Hebrew verb פָּקַח under פקח with its Niphal sense attested in Genesis 3:5.
draft.definition: In the Niphal, eyes are opened, enabling a person to perceive what was previously unrecognized.
draft.evidence: In Genesis 3:5 the serpent links the opening of the hearers’ eyes with knowing good and evil.

analysis.evidence: The feminine plural verb agrees with עֵינֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם, “the eyes of both of them.” The next clause identifies what they recognized when their eyes were opened: they knew they were naked.
analysis.morphology: Niphal wayyiqtol, third-person feminine plural, with prefixed וַ־.
analysis.sense: For eyes to be opened so that a person perceives something previously unrecognized.

analysis.evidence: עֵינֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם means “the eyes of both of them.” The next clause, וַיֵּדְעוּ כִּי עֵירֻמִּם הֵם (“and they knew that they were naked”), identifies the awareness they gained when their eyes opened.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, dual construct, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: עֵינֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם means “the eyes of both of them.” The suffix ־הֶם refers to the man and the woman, who are also the subject of וַיֵּדְעוּ (“they knew”).
analysis.morphology: Masculine dual cardinal numeral in the construct state with a third-person masculine plural pronominal suffix.

analysis.evidence: After the eyes of both were opened, the כִּי clause states what they realized: עֵירֻמִּם הֵם, “they were naked.”
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine plural, with prefixed וַ.
analysis.sense: to know that something is the case

analysis.evidence: After וַיֵּדְעוּ (“they knew”), כִּי introduces עֵירֻמִּם הֵם (“they were naked”), the clause stating what the two knew.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected subordinating conjunction with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: that (what is seen, known or said)

analysis.evidence: The initial עֵי־ in עֵירֻמִּם identifies the plural of עֵירֹם. In כִּי עֵירֻמִּם הֵם, the two realize that they are naked, then sew fig leaves together to make coverings for themselves.
analysis.morphology: Adjective, masculine plural absolute, used predicatively with הֵם.

analysis.evidence: In כִּי עֵירֻמִּם הֵם (‘that they were naked’), הֵם is the subject and עֵירֻמִּם is the predicate. The pronoun refers to the two people just mentioned in שְׁנֵיהֶם (‘both of them’).
analysis.morphology: Independent personal pronoun, third person masculine plural.

draft.change: Add the Hebrew Qal verb תָּפַר with the sense “sew together.”
draft.evidence: In Genesis 3:7 the two sew fig leaves together to make waist coverings.

analysis.evidence: The verb takes עֲלֵה תְאֵנָה, “fig leaves,” as its direct object. The next clause gives the result: the two made waist coverings for themselves. The leaves are the material they stitched together.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third masculine plural, with prefixed וַ־ and plural ending ־וּ.

analysis.evidence: In עֲלֵה תְאֵנָה, the construct noun names the leaves and תְאֵנָה identifies the fig tree. The pair sew the fig leaves together to make coverings for themselves.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct noun, used collectively.

draft.change: Add תְּאֵנָה under its own consonants, תאנה, with distinct senses for the tree and its fruit.
draft.definition: The fig tree, or the fig it bears. In Genesis 3:7 the noun denotes the tree.
draft.evidence: Genesis 3:7 identifies the tree by its leaves. Proverbs 27:18 speaks of tending a תְּאֵנָה and eating its fruit. Jeremiah 24:2 uses the plural for the figs in two baskets.

analysis.evidence: In עֲלֵה תְאֵנָה, “leaves of a fig tree,” עֲלֵה is the plural construct of עָלֶה. תְאֵנָה names the tree whose leaves the couple sewed together.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, feminine singular absolute, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: חֲגֹרֹת names what they made, waist coverings, and לָהֶם means “for themselves.” The preceding clause describes how they made the coverings by sewing fig leaves together.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third masculine plural, with prefixed וַ.

analysis.evidence: After the two realize they are naked, they sew fig leaves together. In וַיַּעֲשׂוּ לָהֶם חֲגֹרֹת, the plural noun names the waist coverings they made for themselves.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, feminine plural absolute, without prefix or suffix
